title: Classification: Predicting Yes/No
subtitle: Logistic regression as odds, kNN and Naive Bayes as contrasts, the confusion matrix in depth, precision vs. recall, ROC vs. PR — on 30,000 credit-card customers, 22% of whom default

objectives.title: Read Logistic Regression as Odds
objectives.description: The sigmoid turns a linear score into a probability; each coefficient is a log-odds change. e^0.69 ≈ 2 means 'doubles the odds' — the sentence a credit officer can repeat.

objectives.title: Contrast Three Classifiers
objectives.description: Logistic regression draws a line, kNN votes among neighbors, Naive Bayes multiplies likelihoods. Same data, three decision boundaries, three sets of strengths.

objectives.title: Master the Confusion Matrix
objectives.description: Four cells, four business meanings. Precision, recall, F1, specificity — computed by hand once, so you never again trust a single accuracy number.

objectives.title: Choose ROC-AUC or PR-AUC
objectives.description: ROC for balanced problems and ranking quality; precision–recall when the positive class is rare and false alarms cost money. Fraud at 0.2% makes the difference brutal.

agenda.title: HW2 Debrief & Meet the Data: Credit-Card Default
agenda.description: Three residual plots from your Ames submissions, then a new dataset: 30,000 credit-card customers in Taiwan, six months of bill and payment history, and a label for whether they defaulted the following month. 22.1% did.
bulletPoints: Baseline: 'nobody defaults' is 77.9% accurate and would bankrupt the bank
Features: credit limit, age, six months of payment status, bill amounts, payment amounts

agenda.title: Logistic Regression: A Line in Log-Odds
agenda.description: Why linear regression fails on a 0/1 target, the sigmoid that fixes it, and coefficients as log-odds. Payment status last month has the biggest coefficient — and exponentiating it tells you exactly how much a late payment multiplies the odds of default.
bulletPoints: predict_proba gives the probability; predict just applies a 0.5 cutoff you never chose
C is inverse regularization strength: it's ridge/lasso for classification

agenda.title: kNN & Naive Bayes: Two Other Ways to Draw a Boundary
agenda.description: kNN: no training, just voting among the k nearest customers — and a decision boundary that follows the data everywhere. Naive Bayes: multiply likelihoods, fast and surprisingly good on text. Decision-boundary plots on two features make the three models' personalities visible.
bulletPoints: kNN needs scaling and gets slow at scale; k controls bias–variance exactly like polynomial degree
Naive Bayes assumes independence it doesn't have — and often works anyway

agenda.title: Break
agenda.description: Stretch, coffee, pick a competition teammate — the midterm launches next week.

agenda.title: The Confusion Matrix, Cell by Cell
agenda.description: True positive: a defaulter we flagged. False negative: a defaulter we approved — the expensive cell. False positive: a good customer we declined — the cell that loses revenue and trust. Precision, recall, F1, specificity computed by hand, then classification_report.
bulletPoints: Precision: of those we flagged, how many defaulted? Recall: of those who defaulted, how many did we flag?
F1 is the harmonic mean — useful, but it assumes both mistakes cost the same. They never do

agenda.title: ROC vs. Precision–Recall & Class Imbalance
agenda.description: The ROC curve sweeps every threshold and plots recall against false-positive rate; AUC is the probability a random defaulter scores above a random good customer. Then the PR curve — and why at 22% default ROC is fine, but at 0.2% fraud only PR tells the truth. class_weight='balanced' as the first fix for imbalance; why SMOTE is usually unnecessary.
bulletPoints: Logistic regression on this data: AUC ≈ 0.72 with raw features, ≈ 0.77 with the payment-status columns treated as categories
Imbalance fixes in order: choose the right metric, reweight, tune the threshold (next week), then and only then resample

agenda.title: Wrap-Up: The Cliffhanger
agenda.description: We now have a probability for every customer. We have not decided what to do with it. predict() used 0.5 — who chose that? Next week: costs, thresholds, calibration, and profit curves. HW3 launches.
bulletPoints: HW3 (due Nov 2): a credit-default classifier with a threshold you can defend — Session 6 gives you the tools

activities.title: Who Defaults Next Month? Three Classifiers, One Confusion Matrix
activities.description: 30,000 credit-card customers, 22% default rate. Fit logistic regression, kNN, and Gaussian Naive Bayes in the same pipeline, compare ROC-AUC and PR-AUC, and then read the logistic model's confusion matrix cell by cell in the bank's language.

steps.title: Frame it
steps.description: Unit: one cardholder. Target: default next month. Horizon: one month. Decision: reduce the credit line / call / do nothing. Baseline: 77.9% accuracy by predicting 'no default' for everyone.

steps.title: Fit three models in one pipeline
steps.description: Same preprocessing, swap the last step: LogisticRegression, KNeighborsClassifier(k=25), GaussianNB. Record ROC-AUC and average precision for each.

steps.title: Read the odds
steps.description: np.exp(coef_) for the logistic model. Find the feature with the largest odds ratio and say it in a sentence a credit officer would understand.

steps.title: Read the matrix
steps.description: Confusion matrix at the default threshold. Name each cell in business terms. Compute precision and recall by hand, then confirm with classification_report.

codeBlock.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_openml
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, average_precision_score, confusion_matrix

credit = fetch_openml(data_id=42477, as_frame=True)
X, y = credit.data, (credit.target == '1').astype(int)      # 1 = defaulted next month
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=835)

models = {
    'logistic': LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000),
    'knn-25':   KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=25),
    'naive bayes': GaussianNB(),
}
for name, clf in models.items():
    pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), clf).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    p = pipe.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
    print(f'{name:12s} ROC-AUC {roc_auc_score(y_te, p):.3f}   PR-AUC {average_precision_score(y_te, p):.3f}')

logit = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(confusion_matrix(y_te, logit.predict(X_te)))   # rows: actual, cols: predicted

activities.discussionNote: The three models rank customers similarly (AUC within a few points) — but look at the confusion matrix: at the default threshold, logistic regression flags only a fraction of the defaulters. That is not a modeling failure. It is a decision nobody made: predict() silently assumes a missed default costs the same as a wrongly declined customer. Next week we price the two mistakes and let the price choose the threshold.

takeaways.text: Logistic regression is linear in log-odds: exponentiate a coefficient to get an odds ratio, and say it in words — 'a late payment last month roughly doubles the odds of default.'

The confusion matrix has four cells with four business meanings. Precision asks 'of those we flagged…', recall asks 'of those who actually…'. Accuracy averages over both mistakes and hides which one you are making.

ROC-AUC measures ranking; PR-AUC measures usefulness on rare positives. At 22% default either works; at 0.2% fraud only precision–recall tells the truth. And predict()'s 0.5 threshold is a decision you have not yet made.
